first.rationale: Two of the current problems (activation down 6%, onboarding completion down 4%) map directly onto prior consolidated findings that reducing signup friction (memory_31) and shortening onboarding (memory_86) durably improved these exact metrics. With only one experiment slot, addressing the internally-caused, directly measurable regressions is higher-confidence and lower-risk than reacting to competitor pricing pressure, which risks a margin-eroding race to the bottom that harms 'sustainable long-term qualified revenue' even if it recovers short-term SMB volume (promotional pricing memory_73 was about acquisition/revenue lift, not tested against an active price war or long-term margin impact). Referral incentives and enterprise sales-assist don't address this quarter's acute regressions. I verify memory_31 and memory_86 because they are the two memories the intended action directly depends on and because two independent archived studies converging on the same lever warrants confirming neither was a narrow or confounded result before committing scarce experiment capacity. I'm treating this as a standard experiment rather than broad rollout because although history supports the direction, current-quarter causal attribution (is the drop due to a design regression, seasonality, or competitive spillover reducing signup quality?) hasn't been re-verified, so I preserve uncertainty about whether the historical lift will fully reproduce now.

final.rationale: Archive confirms both memories as accurate to their original claims: exp_31 (signup simplification) drove activation +9% and qualified revenue +4% on SMB, though with a small -1% retention dip, and was explicitly noted as not replicated outside SMB; exp_86 (shortened onboarding) confirmed completion +13%, faster time-to-value, and positive +3% retention. Together these map cleanly onto this quarter's two internally-diagnosable regressions (activation -6%, onboarding completion -4%), giving a stronger causal and evidentiary basis than the competitor-pricing-driven urge to match promotional pricing, which risks race-to-bottom margin erosion against 'sustainable long-term qualified revenue' and has no confirmed record under active-price-war conditions. I proceed with simplify_onboarding (which functionally bundles the signup/onboarding friction reduction validated by both sources) as a standard_experiment rather than broad_rollout: exp_31's benefit was confirmed only for SMB and carried a slight retention cost, so scaling broadly without re-validating on the current mixed segment mix and under new competitive dynamics would outrun the evidence. I flag downstream_value_risk because exp_31's -1% retention dip, even though net-positive on revenue historically, means the retention/revenue tradeoff should be monitored this cycle rather than assumed to hold given the added complication of aggressive competitor pricing pulling on the same SMB segment. Uncertainty is preserved: this is a single-week, standard-scale experiment, not a rollout decision, and results should be re-assessed before any broader commitment or before addressing the pricing threat separately.
